t: Form Array by Concatenating Subarrays of Another Array - Greedy Sequential Matching
o: Think of `nums` as a tape consumed strictly left to right: the i-th chunk cut from it must equal `groups[i]` exactly; chunks may be separated by unused elements but can neither overlap nor appear out of order. Example 1 succeeds: `[1,-1,-1]` matches at index 3 and `[3,-2,0]` follows immediately at index 6. Example 2 fails purely on order - `[10,-2]` appears after `[1,2,3,4]`, not before. Example 3 fails on disjointness: the only way to see `[1,2,3]` ends at index 4, forcing `[3,4]` to reuse `nums[4]`. The key realization is that matching the current group as early as possible never hurts: it leaves the maximal suffix for later groups. Sizes are tiny (everything <= 10^3), so naive scanning is ample, though KMP upgrades the match to linear time.
k: Greedy earliest-match is optimal: if any valid placement exists, the one taking each group's first feasible start also exists.
After placing groups[0..i], only the suffix of nums past the last placed chunk matters.
Each group is an exact contiguous pattern, so this decomposes into sequential string matching - KMP makes each search linear.

a.i: March one pointer through nums. For the current group, advance until the window starting at the pointer equals the group, then jump the pointer past the matched block and move to the next group. If nums runs out first, return false. Correctness follows from an exchange argument: any solution that places the current group later than the greedy choice can be shifted earlier without colliding, since prior groups end even further left.
s: For each group g, advance i while the window nums[i..i+len(g)) does not equal g (bounds-checked).
If i leaves the array, return false; otherwise jump i to the end of the matched window.
Return true once every group is placed.
a.t: O(sum(|groups|) * m) worst case - each group rescans up to the whole array; about 10^6 operations at the given limits.
a.sp: O(1) auxiliary space beyond transient slices in some languages.

a.i: Treat each group as a pattern over an alphabet of integers and run Knuth-Morris-Pratt from the current position: build the failure function once per group, then scan nums with amortized O(1) work per element. The earliest match returned by KMP coincides exactly with what greedy needs, and on success we resume just past it. This removes the worst-case quadratic behavior of naive re-comparison while keeping the same outer logic.
s: Precompute the failure (prefix) function of the current group.
Scan nums starting at pointer i with automaton state k.
On a full match, resume at the position right after it with k reset; if nums ends first, return false.
Repeat for all groups; return true.
a.t: O(m + sum(|groups|)) time - each element of nums advances the state with amortized O(1) failure-link hops per pattern.
a.sp: O(maxGroupLen) space for the failure tables.

w: Default to the greedy scan and spend the saved effort arguing correctness via the exchange argument. Pitfalls: advancing the pointer by 1 instead of len(g) after a match (breaks disjointness - exactly Example 3), forgetting the tail-bounds check when the remaining slice is shorter than the next group, and assuming subsequence semantics rather than contiguous chunks. Follow-ups: many patterns searched simultaneously (Aho-Corasick), patterns that may be skipped or reused, or streaming input where you must answer incrementally.
